Chapter 4: The Power of Honest Feedback and the Braintrust Model
As the studio took on bigger and more ambitious projects, something became impossible to ignore—the need for honest, constructive feedback.
If you’ve ever worked in a typical organization, you know how tricky feedback can be. People tiptoe around the truth, not wanting to hurt anyone’s feelings, and sometimes, criticism gets softened so much that it loses all its meaning.
But here’s the thing—when you’re creating animated films, every tiny detail matters. Sugarcoating the truth? That can spell disaster.
There was a real turning point during the development of a major film. The story just wasn’t working, and honestly, the whole team could feel it. But every time they met to talk about what was wrong, the conversations stayed polite and… well, kind of superficial. No one wanted to be the person who really called out the issues. So the project drifted, and the sense of urgency faded.
Clearly, something had to give. The solution? A whole new kind of meeting. Imagine a room where titles and hierarchies got left at the door. The only thing that mattered was the work itself. People were encouraged—actually expected—to speak their minds, challenge assumptions, and offer honest feedback, even if it was uncomfortable.
At first, it felt awkward. Old habits are tough to break, and it took time for everyone to trust that speaking up wouldn’t get them in trouble. But as these meetings continued, something pretty amazing happened. Feedback got sharper, discussions went deeper, and solutions started to pop up that no one had considered before. Suddenly, problems that once seemed impossible started to unravel, and the project found its footing again.
This practice became known as the Braintrust—a new way to solve problems together that became central to the studio’s success. The magic wasn’t just about having smart people in the room—it was about creating a culture where candor was the norm, and everyone felt safe to speak freely. In the Braintrust, nobody had all the answers, and every perspective was genuinely valued.
One moment really stands out: a team member, clearly nervous but determined, pointed out a flaw in the story that everyone else had missed. There was a pause—one of those moments where time seems to stop. But instead of defensiveness, the room filled with curiosity. The group leaned in, explored the issue from every angle, and eventually found a solution that made the film stronger. It just goes to show, the best ideas often come from the most unexpected places—and honest feedback is the real engine behind creativity.
Over time, the Braintrust model grew beyond just story meetings. It became a mindset—a commitment to transparency and open communication that touched every corner of the studio. Leaders even went out of their way to seek out dissenting opinions, because they knew the truth might be uncomfortable, but it was always necessary.
Lots of companies talk about the value of feedback, but very few actually create the conditions for it to happen. It takes real humility, patience, and a willingness to be vulnerable. But if you’re willing to do the work, the rewards are huge. Problems get solved faster, ideas get better, and the whole team grows stronger together.
Looking back, it’s clear that the Braintrust wasn’t just another meeting—it became a symbol for the kind of culture the studio wanted to build. A place where honesty matters more than politeness, where the work is more important than anyone’s ego, and where everyone feels empowered to make a difference.
